330.title: Ravana lifts the mountain
330.hook: Ravana tries to lift Shiva's mountain and ends up singing under it; why a temple's peak is for bowing
330.carry: the ego lifts; the devotee bows
330.howItsDone: Many Hindus bow on entering a temple, before the shrine and before elders, and touch an elder's feet for a blessing; the Kailasa temple at Ellora, cut from a single rock, carries a famous carving of Ravana shaking Kailash.

segments.voice: Yesterday: abhaya mudra, the raised open palm that says don't be afraid. Your line was your worth isn't up for a vote: abhaya, no fear. Today, the top of year one.

Ravana is flying home in the Pushpaka, the flying chariot he has just taken from his own half-brother, and he has never been more sure of himself. Then, over a mountain in the far north, the chariot stops dead. It won't go on. Shiva's attendant Nandi steps out. This is Kailash, he says. Shiva and Parvati are here. Go around. Ravana laughs. Go around? He climbs down, gets his twenty arms under the mountain, and lifts.
screen: `THE CHARIOT STOPS OVER KAILASH.` → `GO AROUND.` → `RAVANA LIFTS THE MOUNTAIN.`

segments.voice: The mountain shakes. Parvati catches hold of Shiva. And Shiva, without even getting up, presses down with one toe. The mountain settles, and Ravana's arms are pinned beneath it. He roars with pain so loud the worlds tremble. His ministers tell him there's only one way out: praise the one you tried to move. So, pinned under the mountain, he sings to Shiva, and the old telling says he sang for a thousand years. At last Shiva lets him go and gives him a name: Ravana, the one who roared. At Ellora, in western India, a whole temple is cut down into one cliff of rock and named for Kailash itself, and on its side Ravana shakes the mountain while Shiva calmly holds it still with his foot. That's the shikhara idea: a temple's tower is often said to echo a holy mountain, Kailash or Meru. You don't climb it and stand on top. You come in under it, to the small dark room at its heart, and you bow. Hindus have a name for the part of you that tries to lift the mountain, and many teachers read Ravana here as just that: ahamkara, the I-maker, the ego that says mine, I did it. Ravana was strong enough to shake Kailash. Strength just wasn't the way in. Bowing was. Today is the top of year one: words, stories, practices, a whole scripture read through, the depths. The ahamkara would love to stand up here and say, done, I've got this. The tradition's move is the other one. At the top, you bow.
screen: `ONE TOE, AND THE MOUNTAIN SETTLES.` · `RAVANA, THE ONE WHO ROARED.` · `THE SHIKHARA ECHOES THE MOUNTAIN.` · `AHAMKARA: THE I-MAKER.` · `THE TOP OF YEAR ONE.` · then, large: `AT THE TOP, YOU BOW.`

segments.voice: Let the year come back in a few pictures: a word, a story, a flame. Notice the small voice that wants to say I did that. Then do what Hindus do on entering a temple or meeting an elder: bow, in your body if you can, or in your mind. If you pray, offer the whole year back to God. If you don't, simply let it be bigger than you, and rest there.
Shikhara, a mountain peak, and the name for the tower over a north Indian temple's shrine, often said to echo the holy mountain. You don't stand on it. You come in under it, and bow.
Your line: the ego lifts; the devotee bows. Ravana learned it under Kailash. Day three hundred thirty.

331.title: Parvati in the snows
331.hook: the daughter of the mountain wins Shiva with years of tapas, not tricks; why women fast on Teej
331.howItsDone: On Hartalika Teej many Hindu women fast, some without water, and worship Shiva and Parvati in memory of her tapas; others keep vrats, vowed fasts, such as Monday fasts for Shiva.

segments.voice: Yesterday: shikhara, and Ravana pinned under Kailash until he sang. Your line was the ego lifts; the devotee bows.

Himalaya, the mountain king, has a daughter, and her name tells you whose she is: Parvati, daughter of the mountain. She has set her heart on Shiva, who sits on Kailash smeared in ash, eyes closed, wanting nothing. The gods already tried to wake him with Kama, the god of love, and it went badly: one look from Shiva's third eye, and Kama was ash. So Parvati stops trying to be noticed. She does something much harder.
screen: `THE DAUGHTER OF THE MOUNTAIN.` → `KAMA, BURNED TO ASH.` → `SHE DOES SOMETHING HARDER.`

segments.voice: She climbs into the high snows and begins tapas: the heat of a practice kept up, day after day. In the poet Kalidasa's telling, she stands in icy water on winter nights and sits between fires under the summer sun. She eats less and less, until she lives on fallen leaves, and then gives up even those. That's why one of her names is Aparna: the one without even a leaf. Years pass. Then a young ascetic with matted hair walks into her clearing. Why waste yourself on Shiva? he asks. He lives in cremation grounds. He wears snakes. Parvati's eyes flash. You don't know him, she says. My heart is set, and I won't hear another word. She turns to go. And the stranger stops her: he is Shiva himself, in disguise. From today, he says, I'm yours, won by your tapas. Hindus still keep this story, with a fast. On Hartalika Teej, many women, especially in north India, Maharashtra and Nepal, fast all day, some without even water, in memory of Parvati's tapas, and worship Shiva and Parvati together. The teaching is tapas: steady effort, offered to God, is a heat that burns something away. Parvati didn't win Shiva by being noticed. She won him by keeping going. Now look back at your year. Three hundred thirty-one days, a few minutes each, mostly unseen. That's a small tapas. And from here you can see the next range: tomorrow, year two opens an Upanishad that begins with one sound, om.

segments.voice: Last sit of year one. Sit tall, the way Parvati sat in the snow. Think of one small thing you kept up this year, a minute a day, a lamp, a word, a habit, and feel the warmth it built; tapas means heat. If you pray, offer it to Shiva and Parvati, or to God by whatever name you use, and ask for steadiness for the next range. If you don't, just thank the you who kept showing up.
Himalaya, the abode of snow: Parvati's father, the mountain king, and the snows where she kept her tapas. The next range is behind it, and you climb it the way she did, one day at a time.
Your line: tapas, love that keeps going. That's day three hundred thirty-one, and year one.

332.title: Om, the essence of essences
332.hook: year two opens the Chandogya Upanishad, and its very first line says: meditate on om, the high chant
332.tomorrow: speech and breath argue about who is greatest
332.howItsDone: Many Hindus chant om at the start and end of prayer, study and puja; in traditional Vedic schools, students of the Sama Veda still learn the Chandogya's chants by ear from a teacher.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Himalaya, and Parvati in the snows, and your line, tapas: love that keeps going. Year two starts now, with the first range.

Year two opens beside a fire. In the old Vedic sacrifice, priests sit around a fire on an altar, each with a job. One pours the offerings. One recites the verses. And one, the singer, waits for his moment, then lifts his voice into a long, rising chant: the udgitha, the high song. It was his whole craft. Now suppose someone in that circle asked a strange question. Not how do you sing it, but what is it, really? What is the song made of? The Chandogya Upanishad, where year two begins, opens with an answer.
screen: `A FIRE, A CIRCLE OF PRIESTS.` → `THE SINGER'S HIGH SONG.` → `WHAT IS IT MADE OF?`

segments.voice: The Chandogya belongs to the Sama Veda, the Veda of chants, so of course it starts with singing. Its first words are om ity etad aksharam udgitham upasita. Roughly: meditate on this syllable, om, as the udgitha. The high song and the sacred syllable are one. Then the text builds a ladder of essences. The essence of all these beings is the earth. Of earth, water. Of water, plants. Of plants, the human person. Of the person, speech. Of speech, the verses of the Rig Veda. Of the verses, the chant of the Sama Veda. And the essence of the chant is the udgitha, which is om. Then comes the line the whole day turns on: the udgitha is rasanam rasatamah, the essence of essences, the highest, the eighth rung. Rasa means juice, sap, flavor, the best part of a thing. Follow it down again: soil, rain, rice, a person, a voice, a verse, a song, a single syllable. In the text's picture, a person, boiled down, ends in a sound. That's the Upanishad's move, and you'll see it all year: it takes something the priests already did, a song at a fire, and asks what it means on the inside. The ritual stays. The meaning goes deeper. Om still opens prayer, study and puja in Hindu homes and temples today, and this chapter is one place that asks why.
screen: `THE VEDA OF CHANTS BEGINS WITH A SONG.` · `OM AND THE HIGH SONG ARE ONE.` · `A LADDER: EARTH TO WATER TO PERSON.` · `THE ESSENCE OF ESSENCES.` · then, large: `RASANAM RASATAMAH.`

segments.voice: Climb the ladder in your mind: the ground under you, the water you drank today, the food it grew, your body made from that food, your voice. If you'd like, let one soft om come out on the breath, or simply hear it inside, and notice it begin, swell and fade. Then rest in the quiet after it, the way the text rests at the top of its ladder.
The udgitha. The high song of the Sama Veda priests, which the Chandogya identifies with om and calls the essence of essences.
Your line: om, the essence of essences. Boil a prayer down and this is what's left, so it comes first. Year two has begun.

333.title: The senses walk out
333.hook: the senses quarrel over which of them matters most, and they settle it by leaving the body one at a time
333.carry: prana: the breath that holds the rest
333.howItsDone: Many Hindus practice pranayama, the regulation of breath, before worship and in yoga; when an image is installed in a temple or home shrine, the rite of prana pratishtha 'sets the breath' in it.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the udgitha, om, om: the essence of essences of essences: earth, water, plants, person, speech, verse, chant, om. Your line was om, the essence of essences.
screen: `OM: OM: THE ESSENCE OF ESSENCES OF ESSENCES.`

segments.voice: Sooner or later, every team has this argument. The one who talks to the clients says the company runs on them. The one who builds the product says nothing exists without them. The planner says without a plan it's all chaos. The Chandogya Upanishad tells the same fight, only the team is inside your own body: speech, the eye, the ear, the mind and the breath, arguing over which of them is the greatest. The way they settle it is brilliant, and a little brutal.
screen: `EVERY TEAM HAS THIS ARGUMENT.` → `THE TEAM IS YOUR BODY.` → `WHO IS THE GREATEST?`

segments.voice: They go to Prajapati, the lord of creatures, and ask him to judge. His test: the greatest is the one whose leaving makes the body worst off. So they take turns walking out. Speech leaves for a whole year. Back again, it asks how they managed. Like someone who can't speak, the others say. We breathed, we saw, we heard, we thought. We got by. The eye leaves for a year, and they get by like someone who can't see. The ear leaves, and they live like someone who can't hear. The mind leaves, and they live, the text says, like small children whose minds haven't grown yet. Each time, the body carries on. Then breath gets ready to go. And here's the picture that makes the story stick: as a strong horse, pulling away, tears up the pegs it was tethered to, the breath begins to tear up all the others with it. Speech, eye, ear and mind come running. Stay, they say. You're the greatest of us. That full story sits in chapter five of the Chandogya. Chapter one has a shorter one: gods and demons fight, and the demons spoil speech, eye, ear and mind with evil. But when they strike the breath in the mouth, the chief breath, they shatter like a clod of earth thrown at a rock. In both places, breath holds the rest. And chapter five ends by saying people don't call the senses speech, eyes, ears and minds. They call them all pranas, breaths. That's why breath is treated as sacred: many Hindus begin worship with pranayama, tending the breath, and when a temple image is consecrated, the rite is prana pratishtha, setting the breath in.
screen: `PRAJAPATI'S TEST: WHO CAN LEAVE?` · `SPEECH, EYE, EAR, MIND: THE BODY GETS BY.` · `THE HORSE TEARS UP ITS PEGS.` · `THE SENSES ARE CALLED BREATHS.` · `PRANAYAMA. PRANA PRATISHTHA.` · then, large: `PRANA HOLDS THE REST.`

Prana, life-breath. When breath prepares to leave the body, like a strong horse tearing up its tethering pegs, speech, eye, ear and mind come running, calling it the greatest of them all.
Your line: prana, the breath that holds the rest. The others can step out for a year; breath can't. Day three hundred thirty-three, done.

334.title: The dogs who chanted for breakfast
334.hook: a pack of dogs files in like priests, sits down, and chants: om, let us eat; om, let us drink
334.carry: bhava: the chant needs its inside
334.tomorrow: Satyakama, the boy who told the truth
334.howItsDone: Hindu teachers often stress bhava, the inner feeling behind worship, alongside correct form; many families teach children both the words of a prayer and what it means.

segments.voice: Yesterday: prana, and your line, the breath that holds the rest. The senses walked out one by one, but when breath pulled away like a horse tearing up its pegs, they all came running back.
screen: `PRANA — THE BREATH THAT HOLDS THE REST.`

segments.voice: A student walks out of the village to study the Veda somewhere quiet, and a white dog appears in front of him. Other dogs gather around the white dog and say to it: sir, sing for us, and get us some food. We're hungry. The white dog says: come back here tomorrow morning. The student, understandably, stays to watch. Next morning the dogs return, and what they do is not what you'd expect to find in a book of sacred chant.
screen: `A STUDENT GOES TO STUDY.` → `A WHITE DOG, AND A HUNGRY PACK.` → `COME BACK TOMORROW.`

segments.voice: The dogs come in a line, each holding on to the one ahead, the way the priests moved together when they entered to sing a particular chant. They sit down. They make the chant's opening sound, hin. Then they sing, in the same form the priests used for the high song we met two days ago. Om, let us eat. Om, let us drink. Om, may the gods bring food here. Lord of food, bring food here, bring it. Om. That's the whole hymn. Two days ago the Chandogya called this chant the essence of essences. Now a pack of dogs uses the exact same chant to ask for breakfast. Many modern scholars read the passage as satire: a sharp joke at priests who sang the sacred song mainly for the fee and the meal that came with it. The words and form were right. What was missing was the inside, the meditation the first chapter asked for. Not everyone reads it as a joke. Some traditional commentators take the dogs as sages or gods in disguise, come to teach the student. The text doesn't explain itself, so both readings stay open. Either way, the Chandogya's own refrain points the same direction: again and again it promises its fruit to ya evam veda, the one who knows this. Hindu teachers call that inside bhava, the feeling and meaning you bring. And the question lands on anyone who has said grace while thinking about dessert, or sung a hymn while checking the time. You can do every outward step of a ritual and still be chanting for food alone.

segments.voice: Take one small thing you do by habit, a prayer before meals, lighting a lamp, even washing your hands, and go through it slowly in your mind, step by step. 335.title: Satyakama at the teacher's door
335.hook: a boy asks his mother who his father was; she doesn't know, and he carries that answer, word for word, to his teacher
335.tomorrow: the bull, the fire, the swan, the bird
335.howItsDone: Satyakama's story is told to Hindu children as a lesson in honesty, and teachers cite it when discussing whether spiritual standing comes from birth or from character.

segments.voice: Yesterday: udgitha, and a pack of dogs chanting om, let us eat. Your line was bhava: the chant needs its inside.

Name. Date of birth. Father's name. On plenty of old forms, that third line sat near the top, and for some people it was the hardest line on the page. In the Chandogya, a boy who wants to study the Veda faces the spoken version of that line. A teacher will ask: what is your family, your lineage? So the boy, Satyakama, goes home first and asks his mother.
screen: `FATHER'S NAME: ______.` → `WHAT IS YOUR LINEAGE?` → `A BOY ASKS HIS MOTHER.`

segments.voice: His mother's name is Jabala, and she answers him honestly. I don't know your lineage, my son. When I was young, I moved about a great deal working as a servant, and that's when I had you. But I am Jabala, and you are Satyakama. So call yourself Satyakama Jabala: a name made from his mother, not his father. The boy walks to the teacher, Haridrumata Gautama, and asks to become his student. The teacher asks: what is your lineage, my dear? And Satyakama repeats his mother's words, all of them, the part that might shame her and the part that might shut him out. I don't know, sir. My mother says she moved about as a servant when she was young, and had me then. She is Jabala, I am Satyakama. I'm Satyakama Jabala. The teacher's reply is the hinge of the story. No one but a true brahmin could speak like that, he says. Fetch the firewood, my dear. I'll take you as a student. You have not gone away from the truth. Look at what counts as the qualification here. Not birth. Not a famous father. The truth, told when a lie would have been easier. His very name holds it: satya means truth, kama means desire. Satyakama, the one who loves truth. Hindus have read this story in different ways. For some, it shows that character is what a brahmin really is. Others, including some traditional commentators, read the teacher as concluding that a boy this truthful must be of brahmin birth after all. Either way, the story keeps the boy at the door, saying I don't know, out loud.
screen: `I DON'T KNOW, MY SON.` · `SATYAKAMA, SON OF JABALA.` · `HE REPEATS IT ALL TO THE TEACHER.` · `YOU HAVE NOT GONE FROM THE TRUTH.` · then, large: `SATYA, TRUTH. KAMA, DESIRE.`

segments.voice: Settle into the breath and think of one true thing about yourself that you usually leave out: something you don't know, something you aren't, a part of your story you skip. You don't have to tell anyone; just let it be true here, without dressing it up or explaining it away. Notice whether it feels heavier hidden, or lighter said.

336.title: Satyakama's four teachers
336.hook: sent off with four hundred thin cows, Satyakama is taught by the herd's bull, the evening fire, a swan and a diving bird
336.howItsDone: Many Hindus greet the rising sun with folded hands or an offering of water, light a lamp at dusk and bow to rivers; teachers tell Satyakama's story to show that Brahman can be met anywhere, and that a teacher still completes the learning.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Satyakama, the boy who said I don't know at the teacher's door. Your line was satya: satya: truth is the qualification. Today ends the first week of year two.

Satyakama has been accepted. You'd expect his first lesson to be a verse, a chant, a teaching by the fire. Instead his teacher picks out four hundred cows, thin and weak, and says: look after these. Satyakama doesn't complain. I won't come back, he says, until they're a thousand. He drives them off into the forest and stays away for years. No teacher. No books. Just cows, grass and sky. And out there, alone, the lessons start arriving, from teachers nobody would have chosen.
screen: `FOUR HUNDRED THIN COWS.` → `NOT BACK UNTIL A THOUSAND.` → `ALONE IN THE FOREST FOR YEARS.`

segments.voice: When the herd reaches a thousand, the bull speaks. Satyakama, we're a thousand now. Take us home, and let me tell you one quarter of Brahman, the great reality. The bull names the four directions, east, west, south, north, and calls that quarter the shining. The fire, it says, will tell him the next. That evening Satyakama lights the fire and pens the cows, and the fire speaks: earth, the air between, the sky, the ocean. That quarter is the endless. The next evening a swan flies down: fire, sun, moon, lightning. The luminous. The evening after, a diving water bird: breath, eye, ear, mind. The quarter that has a home. Four teachers, four quarters: the directions, the worlds, the lights, and his own body. He reaches his teacher's house, and the teacher looks at him and says: your face shines like someone who knows Brahman. Who taught you? Beings other than people, Satyakama answers. But please, teach me yourself. His teacher does, and the text says nothing was left out. That's the teaching: Brahman, the one reality, isn't only at the altar. It shines in the directions, the worlds, the lights, and in your own breath and eyes. Hindus live that when they greet the rising sun, light a lamp at dusk, or bow to a river. And look back at the week: om, breath, a dogs' chant, a boy's truth, and now a herd at evening. Each day, the Chandogya found Brahman somewhere new.
screen: `THE BULL: THE FOUR DIRECTIONS.` · `THE FIRE, THE SWAN, THE DIVING BIRD.` · `YOUR FACE SHINES. WHO TAUGHT YOU?` · `BRAHMAN SHINES IN EVERYTHING.` · then, large: `THE WHOLE WORLD TEACHES BRAHMAN.`

segments.voice: Notice the direction you're facing and the ones behind and beside you, the bull's quarter; then the ground and the air above it, the fire's; then whatever light is around you, the swan's. Come home to your breath, your eyes, your ears and your mind, the diving bird's. No need to hear any voices; just let each one be a teacher for a few breaths.
The bull. The first of Satyakama's four unlikely teachers, who names the four directions as the shining quarter of Brahman.
